extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional designers, and politically engaged legislators
extracted.subtask_description: Critical criteria and principles for assessing constitutions and republican government arrangements, drawn from a historical/political critique of Nedham's 'right constitution' thesis. Focuses on definitional clarity, institutional design, checks and balances, protection of property, and realistic assumptions about human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual interpretation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: To consider the period in which they were written, the circumstances of the times, and the personal character as well as the political situation of the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this precaution when reading political pamphlets or historical writings (example: Mercurius Politicus reprinted 1656). Understand author's motives, audience, and circumstances before accepting their arguments at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise definition of 'the people'
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify who is meant by 'the people' (e.g., 'Such as shall be successively chosen to represent the people').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflation of words and ideas; political propositions depending on 'the people' must define whether this means all inhabitants, a city, or a representative assembly, because each meaning has different implications for governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits of direct popular action
rubrics_metrics.description: The people (as a whole body of a great nation) can never act, consult, or reason together — 'they cannot march five hundred miles, nor spare the time, nor find a space to meet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to critique claims that direct popular sovereignty can function at scale; supports institutional mechanisms (representation, delegation) for large polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and distribution of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not give a single representative assembly all powers (legislative, executive, and judicial); power must be divided so different bodies check each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A constitution should allocate distinct functions (legislative, executive, judicial) and set institutions to 'watch and controul each other.' Historical examples: Roman consulate/senate/people balance; Venice/Bern/Holland as well-checked oligarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of a single body holding all powers
rubrics_metrics.description: If you give a representative assembly all the power, 'they would invade the liberties of the people' — a body with all powers will become oppressive to minorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposals that centralize powers for the risk of majority tyranny; design mechanisms (vetoes, bicameralism, independent judiciary) to prevent such concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority-oppression risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Majorities frequently oppress minorities: 'the majority has eternally, and without one exception, usurped over the rights of the minority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions must anticipate factional conflict and include safeguards (constitutional protections, minority rights, supermajority requirements) so the majority cannot routinely appropriate others' rights. Use historical examples (Caesar, Roman popular leaders) as cautionary precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional protection of property
rubrics_metrics.description: Property is surely a right of mankind as really as liberty; if property is not held sacred by law and public justice, 'anarchy and tyranny commence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess constitutional provisions for secure property rights (debt protections, prohibition on arbitrary confiscation). Beware designs or policies that encourage abolition of debts or equal division of property as leading to social disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional design must not rely on exceptional virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impractical to make a constitution depend on a steady supply of extraordinary, self-sacrificing characters ('Cincinnatus' types); 'to make a law ... by none but such characters ... would be to decree that the business of the world should come to a full stand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor institutional incentives and systemic checks rather than assuming citizens or leaders will consistently exhibit rare civic virtue; historical contrast between admired examples and typical behavior supports this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of public office incentives (burden vs profit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition (ascribed to Nedham): authority should be so constituted 'that it shall be rather a burden than profit to those that undertake it' so only honest public spirits seek office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text critiques this: making office burdensome can invite hypocrites who feign reluctance while seeking private gain, and may lead to betrayal of the public. Evaluate any institutional rule that intentionally discourages officeholding for its secondary effects on who fills offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require constitutional provisions to compel respect for common rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Some provision must be made in the constitution, 'in favour of justice, to compel all to respect the common right, the public good, the universal law, in preference to all private and partial considerations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the constitutional framework includes enforceable rules and institutions (independent courts, rights enforcement mechanisms) that prioritize general justice over factional/private interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical/poetic substitutes for argument
rubrics_metrics.description: When writers on legislation 'have recourse to poetry, their images may be beautiful, but they prove nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating political arguments or constitutional claims, prioritize concrete historical evidence and logical reasoning over emotive imagery or declamatory flourishes (anti-pattern illustrated by Nedham's poetic appeals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for mutual checks among distinct social/political orders
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-ordered constitution relies on councils and orders that are not purely advisory to a single person but stand as mutual checks: set the orders to 'watch and controul each other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider structural arrangements (nobility, magistracies, councils, representative bodies) that limit each other's power; historical examples where elimination of such checks (e.g., destruction of the senate) led to tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of populist flattery and vote-buying
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who make public service appear easy or gratis may 'carry the liberties and properties of their constituents to market, and sell them for very handsome private profit' by flattering and purchasing suffrages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate electoral and campaign rules to prevent vote-buying, demagogic manipulation, and cynical appeal to base passions; institutional safeguards (transparent finance, secret ballot, anti-corruption rules) are relevant.
